title: Emitter-coupled logic
text:
ECL was invented in August 1956 at IBM by Hannon S. Yourke.[1,2] Originally called current-steering logic, it was used in the Stretch, IBM 7090, and IBM 7094 computers.[3] The logic was also called a current-mode circuit.[4] It was also used to make the IBM Advanced Solid Logic Technology (ASLT) circuits in the IBM 360/91.[5,6,7]

Yourke's current switch was a differential amplifier whose input logic levels were different from the output logic levels. "In current mode operation, however, the output signal consists of voltage levels which vary about a reference level different from the input reference level." In Yourke's design, the two logic reference levels differed by 3 volts. Consequently, two complementary versions were used: an NPN version and a PNP version. The NPN output could drive PNP inputs, and vice versa. "The disadvantages are that more different power supply voltages are needed, and both pnp and npn transistors are required."[3]

Instead of alternating NPN and PNP stages, another coupling method employed Zener diodes and resistors to shift the output logic levels to be the same as the input logic levels.

Beginning in the early 1960s, ECL circuits were implemented on monolithic integrated circuits. They consisted of a differential-amplifier input stage to perform logic followed by an emitter-follower stage to drive outputs and shift the output voltages so they will be compatible with the inputs. The emitter-follower output stages could also be used to perform wired-or logic.

Motorola introduced their first digital monolithic integrated circuit line, MECL I, in 1962.[8] Motorola developed several improved series, with MECL II in 1966, MECL III in 1968 with 1-nanosecond gate propagation time and 300 MHz flip-flop toggle rates, and the 10,000 series (with lower power consumption and controlled edge speeds) in 1971.[9]

The MECL 10H family was introduced in 1981.[10]

Fairchild introduced the F100K family in 1975.[11,12]

The ECLinPS ("ECL in picoseconds") family was introduced in 1987.[13] ECLinPS has 500 ps single-gate delay and 1.1 GHz flip-flop toggle frequency.[14] The ECLinPS family parts are available from multiple sources, including Arizona Microtek, Micrel (subsequently acquired by Microchip Technology Inc.), National Semiconductor, and ON Semiconductor.[15]

The high power consumption of ECL meant that it has been used mainly when high speed is a vital requirement. Older high-end mainframe computers, such as the Enterprise System/9000 members of IBM's ESA/390 computer family, used ECL,[16] as did the Cray-1,[17] and first-generation Amdahl mainframes. (Current IBM mainframes use CMOS.[18]) Beginning in 1975, Digital Equipment Corporation's highest performance processors were all based on multi-chip ECL CPUs—from the ECL KL10 through the ECL VAX 8000 and finally the VAX 9000. By 1991, the CMOS NVAX was launched, which offered comparable performance to the VAX 9000 despite costing 1/25 as much and consuming considerably less power.[19] The MIPS R6000 computers also used ECL. Some of these computer designs used ECL gate arrays.
